stem:
An emergency doctor is planning discharge after appropriate observation of a man who survived a heroin overdose. He is alert, has decision-making capacity and agrees to an addiction appointment tomorrow. He lives with a friend who is willing to learn overdose first aid. The man says, “Naloxone saved me.”

What should be added to the discharge plan?

options.label: A
options.text: A naloxone kit kept by him, to use on himself if he becomes drowsy
options.explanation: A person who is overdosing is usually unable to give naloxone to himself. The friend who will be present needs the supply and training.

options.label: B
options.text: Take-home naloxone with overdose-response training for him and his friend
options.explanation: Naloxone at home with a trained person likely to be present is what makes rescue possible. Both he and his friend should know how to recognise an overdose and respond.

options.label: C
options.text: A naloxone prescription to fill after tomorrow’s addiction-clinic appointment
options.explanation: Relapse and overdose can occur before tomorrow’s appointment, and unfilled prescriptions often go unused. He should leave with naloxone in hand.

options.label: D
options.text: Oral naltrexone to take if he relapses, to block any heroin taken
options.explanation: Naltrexone taken after recent heroin use precipitates withdrawal and does not reverse an overdose in progress. It is not a rescue medicine.

options.label: E
options.text: Resuscitation and recovery-position teaching for his friend, without a naloxone kit
options.explanation: Resuscitation skills without naloxone leave his friend unable to reverse opioid respiratory depression. Education and supply belong together.

context: Overdose survivors and likely witnesses should leave with practical access to naloxone and the skills to respond.
